title: Is Using AI for a Literature Review Plagiarism? | AnswerThis
summary: Is using AI for a literature review plagiarism? See where COPE, ICMJE, Elsevier and universities draw the line, with a sample AI disclosure and a safe workflow.
body_markdown:
No. Using AI for a literature review is not plagiarism in itself. Plagiarism means passing off someone else’s words or ideas as your own. Using an AI tool to find papers, summarize studies you then read, or outline your themes does not do that.


It becomes a problem in three situations. You submit AI-written text as your own when your journal or course requires you to disclose it. The AI repeats a source’s wording or argument and you keep it without a citation. Or the AI invents a reference and you cite it. Journals, publishers and universities now spell these rules out, and this guide shows what each one asks, with a sample disclosure you can adapt.


## TL;DR


-


AI help with searching, summarizing papers you read, outlining and editing is allowed by most journals and many courses, usually with a disclosure.


-


Undisclosed AI-written text can count as misconduct even when no sentence is copied. The ICMJE says nondisclosure “may be construed as misconduct in some circumstances.”


-


AI tools cannot be authors, and they cannot be cited as the source of a finding. Cite the paper you read.


-


Fabricated references are a separate offense from plagiarism, and a common one. Check every reference against the real paper.


-


Your course brief or the journal’s guide for authors decides what you must declare. Read it before you start.


## What counts as plagiarism when AI is involved?


It depends on what the tool did and whether you were open about it. The table sorts common uses from safe to risky.


How you used AI


Is it plagiarism?


What to do


Finding candidate papers with an AI search tool


No


Cite the papers you read, not the tool


Summarizing a paper that you then read yourself


No, if you check the summary


Cite the original paper


Brainstorming themes or an outline


Usually no


Disclose it if your journal or course asks


Fixing grammar, spelling and punctuation in your own text


No


Elsevier says basic checks need no declaration


Pasting AI-written paragraphs into your review without saying so


Often treated as misconduct


Disclose it, and rewrite in your own words where required


Keeping AI text that echoes a source’s wording or idea without a citation


Yes


Find the source, then cite it or cut the text


Citing a reference the AI suggested without checking it exists


Fabrication, its own offense


Verify every reference before you cite it


The pattern is simple. Plagiarism is about credit, so the risk rises as the AI’s part in the work becomes invisible to your reader.


## What do journals require?


Most journals build on three policies. They agree on four points: AI cannot be an author, you must disclose how you used it, you stay responsible for every word, and every borrowed idea still needs a real citation.


### COPE


The Committee on Publication Ethics published its[position statement on authorship and AI tools](https://publicationethics.org/node/56046) on 13 February 2023. It says AI tools “cannot meet the requirements for authorship as they cannot take responsibility for the submitted work.” Authors must say which tool they used and how, in the Materials and Methods or a similar section. They remain fully responsible for the content, including the parts an AI produced.


### ICMJE


The[ICMJE recommendations](https://icmje.acponline.org/recommendations/browse/artificial-intelligence/ai-use-by-authors.html) , which many medical journals follow, ask authors to describe AI use in both the cover letter and the submitted work. Two lines matter most for literature reviews. Humans must ensure “appropriate attribution of all quoted material, including full citations,” and “referencing AI-generated material as the primary source is not acceptable.” Authors should also be able to state that their paper contains no plagiarism, including in text and images the AI produced.


### Elsevier


[Elsevier’s policy](https://www.elsevier.com/about/policies-and-standards/generative-ai-policies-for-journals) asks for a separate AI declaration statement at submission, and that statement appears in the published article. AI tools must not be listed or cited as an author. Basic checks of grammar, spelling and punctuation do not need a declaration.


## What do universities say about coursework?


Rules for students vary more, because each course can set its own limits. The[University of Oxford’s guidance on AI in summative assessment](https://academic.admin.ox.ac.uk/node/4542916) , last updated on 26 June 2025, shows where many universities have landed. Submitting work that breaches an assignment’s rules counts as cheating and may count as plagiarism. Suspected unauthorized AI use goes through the usual disciplinary process. Permitted AI use must be acknowledged with the declaration the assignment asks for.


One detail on that page is telling: as of its last update, Oxford had not endorsed any AI detection tool. Misuse is picked up through marking. A clear declaration and a review you can explain in your own words protect you far better than hoping a detector misses something.


## Why AI-written reviews carry extra risk


Literature reviews depend on citations, and that is exactly where general chatbots slip. When[Walters and Wilder (2023)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-41032-5) asked ChatGPT to write 84 short literature reviews, 55% of the GPT-3.5 citations and 18% of the GPT-4 citations were fabricated. Among citations that pointed to real works, 43% of GPT-3.5’s and 24% of GPT-4’s had substantive errors.


A fake reference is not plagiarism in the strict sense. It is fabrication, which most research integrity policies treat at least as seriously. Our guide on[how to check references for AI-fabricated citations](https://answerthis.io/blog/how-to-check-references-for-ai-fabricated-citations) shows a fast way to catch them.


The quieter risk is borrowed ideas. A chatbot can restate the core argument of a well-known paper in fresh words without naming it. The sentence passes a similarity check, yet the idea belongs to someone else. The fix is the habit that makes any review good: trace every claim to a paper you have read, and cite that paper. Research tools that show their sources make this easy. The AnswerThis[AI academic paper search](https://answerthis.io/search-result) answers questions from real papers and links each point to the paper it came from, so the source of every idea is visible from the start.


## How to use AI in a literature review without plagiarizing


1.


Read the rules first. Check your course brief or the journal’s guide for authors for what is allowed and how to declare it.


2.


Use AI to find and sort studies, not to replace reading them. An AI search tool that ties every result to a real paper, like the AnswerThis AI academic paper search, gives you a reading list you can open one by one.


3.


Cite the paper, never the chatbot, for any finding or idea.


4.


Write the synthesis yourself. If you start from an AI draft, rework it until the argument and the wording are yours, and keep your notes.


5.


Verify every reference: title, authors, year, DOI, and that the paper says what your sentence claims. Then format it with a reliable tool such as the[APA, MLA and Chicago citation generator](https://answerthis.io/citation-generator) .


6.


Keep a short log of the tool, the date, what you asked and what you kept. It makes the declaration easy and answers questions later.


7.


Disclose in the form your journal or course asks for.


For a final pass before you hand it in, our[AI writing self-check before you submit](https://answerthis.io/blog/before-you-submit-ai-writing-self-check) covers the questions editors and markers tend to ask.


## A sample AI disclosure for a literature review


Elsevier’s declaration is a good model even if your journal uses different wording. Its template reads: “During the preparation of this work, the author(s) used \[NAME OF TOOL / SERVICE\] in order to \[REASON\]. After using this tool/service, the author(s) reviewed and edited the content as needed and take(s) full responsibility for the content of the published article.”


Filled in for a literature review, it might say: “During the preparation of this work, the authors used \[tool name\] in order to identify candidate studies and draft summaries of their abstracts. After using this tool, the authors read each included study, reviewed and edited the content as needed, and take full responsibility for the content of the published article.”


For coursework, a plainer version usually works: “I used \[tool name\] on \[date\] to search for sources and suggest an outline. I read every source I cite, and the analysis and wording in this review are my own unless quoted and cited.” Swap in whatever your course’s declaration form asks for.


## Will a plagiarism checker flag AI text?


Not reliably, and that cuts both ways. Similarity checkers compare your text with text that already exists, so freshly generated sentences often come back clean. That does not make them allowed. AI detectors try to judge how text was written rather than where it came from, and universities differ on whether they use them at all. Our overview of[AI plagiarism checkers](https://answerthis.io/blog/ai-plagiarism-checker) explains what these tools can and cannot tell you.

## FAQs


### Is it plagiarism to use ChatGPT to summarize articles for a literature review?


No, if you read the articles, check the summaries and cite the original papers. It becomes a problem when the summary replaces your reading and its wording or claims end up in your review without credit.


### Do I have to cite ChatGPT in my literature review?


Not for findings. The ICMJE says AI-generated material is not acceptable as a primary source. Cite the papers instead, and declare the tool the way your journal or course asks.


### Can I list an AI tool as a co-author?


No. COPE, the ICMJE and Elsevier all say AI tools cannot be authors, because they cannot take responsibility for the work.


### Is paraphrasing with AI plagiarism?


Rewording a source with AI help is not plagiarism by itself if you cite the source and your rules allow the tool. An AI paraphrase of a source you do not cite is still plagiarism, however different the words look.


### What happens if I do not disclose AI use?


For journals, the ICMJE says nondisclosure can lead to corrective action and may be treated as misconduct. For students, it usually goes through the university’s academic integrity process, as Oxford’s guidance describes.


Use AI where it saves you time, trace every idea to a real paper, and say what you used. Start your next review with the[AI literature review generator](https://answerthis.io/literature-review-generator) and check each linked source as you go.
